quotes.text: What I hear is a young guy who wants to have some fun running up against a society based on tradition and silly rules. Eddie Cochran didn't whine about it or lock himself in his room, he laughed about the absurdity of it all then went ahead and had fun anyway. The tone he adopts when encountering parents, teachers and other rule-givers is "Man, these people are weirdos."
Eddie Cochran was a fun-poking social critic, a bundle of kinetic energy, a shockingly brilliant guitarist and as sexy as fuck.

His songs are non-conformists anthems just by the attitude he brings to his music. He awakens the little rebel inside all of us—and that little rebel is a lot closer to who we really are than the person we spend most our lives pretending to be.
During that period, captured on the album Singin' to My Baby, Eddie finds himself in the role of straitjacketed Elvis imitator drowned in strings and cutesy wutesy background singers.
This early Liberty period only yielded one top thirty hit: "Sittin' in the Balcony," which should have told the music industry masterminds that they needed to let Eddie do his thing.

While the song is hardly the most angry or aggressive product of the rockabilly era, it is one of its tightest and most tense creations — that frenetic middle section is like Carl Perkins on extra amphetamines, with Eddie playing his solo in a style that ideologically predicts Ten Years After's Alvin Lee: not particularly inventive or challenging, but driving and engaging series of licks, played as fast as possible for head-spinning effect.

This odd alternation of «stuttering» and «speeding» rhythms, I think, was quite deliberately engineered to match the song's lyrics — an even odder tale of struggle and defeat that reads like an extension of old broken-elevator-in-skyscraper jokes and could be interpreted any old way, from a lament on man's fatal dependence on modern technology to an allegory of impotence caused by all of life's troubles.
But since Cochran's general vibe was usually all about how «it's so hard to be a young man in this modern world», I insist on the symbolic significance of the broken elevator.
